questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨3,5,-1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & =3x-\frac{1}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨3,5,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨3y,\,3x-\frac{1}{y},\,-1⟩=⟨3,5,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3cy=3 \\ 3cx-\frac{c}{y}=5 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
3(1)y=3\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
3(1)x-\frac{1}{1}=5\,⟹\,x=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=2$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3xy-\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\  & =3(2)(1)-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1) \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(2,1,6).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx}$ at the point $(2,2,2,6).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{x}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{y}}+\frac{\sqrt{z}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xy}+\sqrt{yz}+\sqrt{zx})=\frac{\sqrt{y}}{2\sqrt{z}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,2):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-6 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,2)+(z-2)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,2) \\ w-6 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+(z-2) \\ w-6 & =x+y+z-6 \\ -x-y-z+w & =0 \\ x+y+z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{xyz}$ at the point $(2,2,4,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{yz}}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{xz}}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{xyz})=\frac{\sqrt{xy}}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,2,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 4}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 4}}{2\sqrt{2}}=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,4) & =\frac{\sqrt{2\cdot 2}}{2\sqrt{4}}=\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-4 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,2,4)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,2,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,2,4) \\ w-4 & =(x-2)+(y-2)+\frac{1}{2}(z-4) \\ w-4 & =x+y+\frac{z}{2}-6 \\ -x-y-\frac{z}{2}+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x+2y+z-2w-4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨0,2,-2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y+{y}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{x}{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨0,2,-2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨0,2,-2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \frac{cx}{y}+2cy=2 \\ -c=-2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0\,⟹\,y=1.
$$

And substituting $c=2$ and $y=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
\frac{2x}{1}+2(2)(1)=2\,⟹\,x=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =(-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡1+{1}^{2} \\  & =0+1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-1,1,1).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x+y-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y-{z}^{2})=-2z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) & =-2(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) \\ w & =(x-1)+y-2(z-1) \\ w & =x+y-2z+1 \\ x+y-2z-w+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$
